en: Dīgha Nikāya 5:
The Kūṭadanta Sutta 1.
The Brahmin Householders of Khāṇumata
Thus have I heard:

at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Magadhans with a large community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, arrived at a brahmin village of the Magadhans named Khāṇumata.
There the Blessed One stayed at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Khāṇumata.
Now at that time, the brahmin Kūṭadanta was residing in Khāṇumata, a place teeming with living beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain—
a royal domain granted by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha as a royal gift and a land bestowed upon brahmins.
At that time, a great sacrifice had been prepared by the brahmin Kūṭadanta.
Seven hundred bulls, seven hundred young bulls, seven hundred heifers, seven hundred goats, and seven hundred rams had been brought to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice.
Then the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour among the Magadhans..."
Accompanied by a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he arrived at Khānumata and was staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Khānumata.
Now, this excellent reputation has arisen concerning the venerable Gotama:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata, departing from Khāṇumata, went forth in groups and crowds toward Ambalaṭṭhikā.
Now at that time, the brahmin Kūṭadanta had gone up to the upper terrace of his palace for his midday rest.
The brahmin Kūṭadanta saw the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata departing from Khāṇumata in groups and crowds, heading toward Ambalaṭṭhikā.
Seeing them, he addressed his steward:
“Why is it, Master Steward, that the brahmin householders of Khānumata have departed from Khānumata, forming groups and gathering in crowds, as they proceed toward Ambalaṭṭhikā?
“There is, sir, a recluse named Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan.
While wandering on tour among the Magadhans with a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, he has arrived at Khānumata.”
He is staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā.
Regarding that venerable Gotama, a sublime report of his reputation has spread abroad: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One:

an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."
"Therefore, we are approaching the venerable Gotama for an audience.
Then, it occurred to the brahmin Kūṭadanta:
"I have indeed heard this:"
‘The ascetic Gotama knows the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.
Yet I do not know the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites,
and I desire to perform a great sacrifice.
“What if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him about the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites?
Then the brahmin Kūṭadanta addressed his steward:
“In that case, my good steward, go to the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata. Having approached them, speak thus to the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata:”
“Master, the brahmin Kūṭadanta says this:
‘May you please wait; the brahmin Kūṭadanta will also go to visit the ascetic Gotama.

“Very well, sir,” that steward replied to the brahmin Kūṭadanta, and he went to where the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata were. Having approached them, he said this to the brahmin householders of Khāṇumata:
“Master, the brahmin Kūṭadanta has said this:
‘May you sirs please wait; the brahmin Kūṭadanta will also go to visit the ascetic Gotama.
2. The Discourse on the Qualities of Kūṭadanta.
Now at that time, many hundreds of brahmins were residing at Khāṇumata,
thinking, "We shall attend the great sacrifice of the brahmin Kūṭadanta.
Those brahmins heard:
“It is said that the brahmin Kūṭadanta will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him.
Then those brahmins went to where the brahmin Kūṭadanta was, and having approached him, they said this to the brahmin Kūṭadanta:
“Is it true, sir, that you will approach the ascetic Gotama to see him?”
“It is thus, sir, that I think:
‘I too shall go to see the ascetic Gotama.
“Do not go, Master Kūṭadanta, to see the ascetic Gotama.”
It is not fitting for Master Kūṭadanta to go to see the ascetic Gotama.
If Master Kūṭadanta were to go to see the ascetic Gotama, Master Kūṭadanta’s reputation would diminish and the ascetic Gotama’s reputation would increase.
Insofar as Master Kūṭadanta’s reputation would diminish and the ascetic Gotama’s reputation would increase, on this account it is not fitting for Master Kūṭadanta to go to see the ascetic Gotama.
The ascetic Gotama, however, is worthy to approach the venerable Kūṭadanta for an audience.

For the venerable Kūṭadanta is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth.
Since the venerable Kūṭadanta is well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side, of pure descent back through seven generations...
For seven generations back, you have been untainted and beyond reproach regarding your lineage;
for this reason, Sir Kūṭadanta, it is not fitting for you to go to see the ascetic Gotama. Rather, it is the ascetic Gotama who ought to come to see you, Sir Kūṭadanta.
For Master Kūṭadanta is wealthy, of great fortune and vast possessions, with abundant wealth and resources, and much gold and silver...

[as above] ...Master Kūṭadanta is a reciter, a bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies (nighaṇḍu) and liturgies (keṭubha), including phonology (sakkharappabheda) and etymology (itihāsa) as the fifth;
he is a master of prosody and grammar, and is unerring in the Lokāyata system and the marks of a Great Man... [as above] ...

For Master Kūṭadanta is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing; he is endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing the form of Brahmā, the grace of Brahmā, and is not insignificant to behold...
[as before] ...For Master Kūṭadanta is virtuous, possessed of the virtue of the elders, and endowed with the virtue of the elders...

[as before] ...For Master Kūṭadanta is a speaker of good words, one whose speech is well-articulated, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and capable of making the meaning understood... [as before] ...
For Master Kūṭadanta is the teacher of many teachers; he teaches the mantras to three hundred young brahmins.
Indeed, many young brahmins from various directions and various countries come into the presence of Master Kūṭadanta, seeking the mantras and desiring to master them... [and so forth].
For Master Kūṭadanta is aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of his life’s span;
whereas the ascetic Gotama is young and has only recently gone forth...
[and so on] ...Master Kūṭadanta is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha... [and so on].
For Master Kūṭadanta is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by the brahmin Pokkharasāti...

[and so on] ...Moreover, Master Kūṭadanta dwells in Khāṇumata—a place teeming with beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted as a royal gift and a brahminical endowment by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
And that Master Kūṭadanta dwells in Khāṇumata, teeming with beings, abundant in grass, timber, water, and grain...
"It is a royal enjoyment, a royal gift, a grant of a brahminical estate given by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha;
for this reason, Master Kūṭadanta does not deserve to go to see the ascetic Gotama.
Rather, it is the ascetic Gotama who deserves to come to see Master Kūṭadanta."
3. Discourse on the Qualities of the Buddha.
When this was said, the brahmin Kūṭadanta said this to those brahmins:
"In that case, sirs, listen to me as well, as to how we ourselves ought to approach the venerable Gotama for an audience."
But it is certainly not fitting for that venerable Gotama to come to see us.
For the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is well-born on both sides, from his mother and from his father, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth.
Furthermore, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well-born on both sides, from his mother and from his father, of pure descent...
For seven generations back on our father’s side, we have been unassailable and beyond reproach regarding our birth; in this respect,
that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us, whereas it is we who ought to go to see that venerable Gotama.
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth into homelessness, having abandoned a great circle of kinsmen...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth into homelessness, having abandoned abundant gold and silver, both that which was stored in the earth and that which was kept above ground...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth from the home life into homelessness while still young, a youth with black hair, endowed with auspicious youthfulness and in the prime of his life..."

"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama went forth from the home life into homelessness, shaving off his hair and beard and donning saffron robes, even though his mother and father were unwilling, weeping with tearful faces. ...

Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is handsome, pleasing to behold, serene, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing a divine form and a divine air, and is no mean sight to behold. ...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is virtuous, possessed of noble virtue, possessed of wholesome virtue, and endowed with wholesome virtue."
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is eloquent, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with polite speech that is distinct, clear, and intelligible in its meaning...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is the teacher of many teachers...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has exhausted sensual lust and is free from fickleness..."
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action, a proponent of performance, one who does not prioritize evil toward the brahmin class...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a high family, an unbroken lineage of kshatriyas...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a wealthy family, possessing great riches and great possessions..."
"Indeed, sir, people come from across kingdoms and across countries to ask questions of the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sir, many thousands of deities have gone for refuge with their lives to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sir, such a glorious report concerning the ascetic Gotama has spread abroad:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
… [and so on] … “Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is one who speaks words of welcome, is kindly, sociable, free from haughtiness, open-faced, and the first to speak. … [and so on] …
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by the four assemblies...
Indeed, sirs, many gods and humans have placed their confidence in the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, in whatever village or town the ascetic Gotama dwells, non-human beings do not harass the people in that village or town..."
"Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is a leader of a community, a leader of a group, a teacher of a group; he is reckoned as the foremost among the various founders of sects.
Furthermore, sirs, the fame of the ascetic Gotama has not arisen in the same manner as the fame of these other ascetics and brahmins arises, whether by this way or that."
Now, the fame of the ascetic Gotama has arisen on account of his unsurpassed perfection in true knowledge and conduct...
Indeed, sirs, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, together with his sons, his wives, his retinue, and his ministers, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, King Pasenadi of Kosala, together with his sons, his wives, his retinue, and his ministers, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, together with his sons, his wife, his retinue, and his kinsmen, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts to the ascetic Gotama...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha...
Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by King Pasenadi of Kosala...
"Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by the brahmin Pokkharasāti...
Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Khāṇumata and is staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Khāṇumata.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins come to our village territory, they are our guests."
“Guests, indeed, must be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by us.
Now, sir, since the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Khānumata and is staying at Ambalaṭṭhikā in Khānumata, the ascetic Gotama is our guest.
And guests, indeed, must be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by us.”
"In this respect, that venerable Gotama does not deserve to come to see us;
rather, we ourselves ought to go to see that venerable Gotama.
So much of the venerable Gotama’s praise do I master, yet the venerable Gotama is not possessed of praise merely to that extent."
"For that venerable Gotama possesses immeasurable beauty.
When this was said, those brahmins said this to the brahmin Kūṭadanta:

"In accordance with the way the venerable Kūṭadanta speaks in praise of the ascetic Gotama, even if that venerable Gotama were staying a hundred leagues from here, it would be quite enough for a clansman endowed with faith to go to see him, even if he had to travel with a sack on his back."
“In that case, sir, let us all go together to visit the ascetic Gotama.

4. The Discourse on King Mahāvijita’s Sacrifice Then the brahmin Kūṭadanta, together with a great company of brahmins, went to Ambalaṭṭhikā where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
Some of the brahmin householders from Khāṇumata also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
others exchanged polite and courteous greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings, some sat down to one side; some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side;
some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side; and some, remaining silent, sat down to one side.
As Kūṭadanta the brahmin was sitting to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, Master Gotama:
'The ascetic Gotama understands the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.'"
"But I do not know the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.
Yet I wish to perform a great sacrifice.
It would be well if Master Gotama were to teach me the threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites."
“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Kūṭadanta replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Once upon a time, brahmin, there was a king named Mahāvijita, who was wealthy, with great riches and vast possessions; he had abundant gold and silver, many articles of value, much wealth and grain, and his treasuries and granaries were full.
Then, brahmin, while King Mahāvijita was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:”

‘I have indeed acquired vast human wealth; having conquered a great circle of the earth, I dwell upon it. What if I were to perform a great sacrifice, which would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time?
Then, brahmin, King Mahāvijita addressed his brahmin domestic priest and said this:
‘Here, brahmin, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:’

“I have indeed attained vast human wealth; having conquered a great circle of the earth, I dwell over it. What if I were to perform a great sacrifice that would be for my long-term welfare and happiness?
“I desire, brahmin, to perform a great sacrifice.
May you instruct me in that which would be for my long-term welfare and happiness.”
When this was said, brahmin, the chaplain brahmin said this to King Mahāvijita:
“Your Majesty’s realm is indeed beset with thorns and oppressed; village destructions are seen, town destructions are seen, city destructions are seen, and highway robberies are seen.
Yet if Your Majesty were to levy taxes in such a realm beset with thorns and oppressed, Your Majesty would thereby be one who does what ought not to be done.”
It may occur to the lord king:
"I shall uproot this thorn in the eye by means of execution, imprisonment, confiscation, censure, or banishment. Yet, such is not the proper way to completely uproot that thorn in the eye.
Those who remain as a remnant of the slain will later harass the king’s realm.
Moreover, by means of this arrangement, there will be the complete eradication of this blindness and lethargy.
Therefore, let your majesty the king provide seed-corn and food to those in your majesty’s kingdom who are intent on agriculture and cattle-rearing;
and let your majesty the king provide capital to those in your majesty’s kingdom who are intent on trade.
"May your majesty the king provide food and wages for those who exert themselves as royal servants in the king’s realm.
When those people are devoted to their own work, they will not harass the king’s realm,
and the king’s revenue will become great."
‘The provinces will be secure, free from thorns, and free from oppression; people will dwell there joyfully and merrily, dancing their children upon their breasts, as if their houses were left open.
‘So be it, sir,’ the brahmin replied to King Mahāvijita. Having assented, King Mahāvijita provided seed-corn and food to those in his realm who exerted themselves in agriculture and cattle-herding.
And to those in his realm who exerted themselves in trade, King Mahāvijita provided capital.
And those who exerted themselves as royal servants in the king’s realm, King Mahāvijita established for them food and wages.
Those people, devoted to their own work, did not harass the king’s realm; and the king’s revenue became great.

The countryside was established in safety, free from thorns, without oppression, and the people lived in joy and gladness, dancing with their children on their breasts, as if living with their houses wide open.
Then, brahmin, King Mahāvijita addressed his brahmin family priest and said this:
“The thorn of my vision has been removed by you, sir; thanks to your arrangements, I have a great store of grain.
The countryside is secure, free from thorns, and free from oppression; the people live in joy and delight, swinging their children in their arms, as if they were living with their houses left open.”
“I wish, brahmin, to perform a great sacrifice.
May you instruct me in that which would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.
4.1. The Four Requisites (Catuparikkhāra)
"In that case, let your majesty the king summon those khattiyas who are his followers in the realm, both the townspeople and the countryfolk, saying: 'Sirs, I wish to perform a great sacrifice;
may you grant me permission for that which may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time. [And likewise] those ministers in your majesty’s realm..."
The courtiers, both those from the towns and those from the countryside... the wealthy brahmins, both those from the towns and those from the countryside...
and the householders and money-lenders, both those from the towns and those from the countryside—let them address your majesty the king thus:
‘Sire, I wish to perform a great sacrifice; may your honors grant me permission, so that it may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.’”

“Yes, sir,” the King Mahāvijita replied to the brahmin family priest. Then the King Mahāvijita addressed those khattiyas who were his followers in the realm, both the town-dwellers and the country-folk:
“Sirs, I wish to perform a great sacrifice. May you grant me permission for that which may lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.
“Let the King perform the sacrifice; it is time for the sacrifice, Great King.”

The ministers of King Mahāvijita—both those from the towns and those from the countryside, including the assembly members, the wealthy brahmins both from the towns and the countryside, and the householders and merchants both from the towns and the countryside—the King addressed them thus:
“Sirs, I wish to perform a great sacrifice. May you grant me permission for that which may be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.
“Let the King perform the sacrifice; it is time for the sacrifice, Great King.”
These four types of consent constitute the requisites for that very sacrifice.
4.2. Eight Requisites:
King Mahāvijita was endowed with eight qualities—
Well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth;
handsome, pleasing, attractive, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, possessing a divine form and a divine grace, of such noble appearance that one cannot look at him enough;
wealthy, of great riches and great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, abundant means and equipment, abundant wealth and grain, and full treasuries and granaries.
One who is powerful, endowed with a fourfold army that is obedient and responsive to his commands, surely overcomes his adversaries by means of his glory.

One who is faithful, a giver, a master of generosity, with doors never closed, acts as a fountain for ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the needy, and beggars, performing meritorious deeds.
One who is learned knows the meaning of various things heard and of various things spoken.
‘This is the meaning of this statement;
this is the meaning of that statement’—he is wise, competent, intelligent, and capable of reflecting upon matters past, future, and present.
King Mahāvijita was endowed with these eight qualities.
Thus, these eight factors also become the requisites for that very sacrifice.
4.3. The Four Requisites:
The brahmin family priest is endowed with four qualities.
Well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth;

a reciter and bearer of the mantras, one who has mastered the three Vedas along with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymology, as well as the histories as the fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and thoroughly versed in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man;
virtuous, possessing the virtue of the elders, and endowed with the virtue of the elders.
A wise, learned, and intelligent man who is either first or second among those offering the sacrifice—
a brahmin serving as a domestic priest endowed with these four factors.
Thus, these four factors also become the requisites for that very sacrifice.
4.4. The Threefold Rite.
Then, brahmin, before the sacrifice, the brahmin chaplain taught King Mahāvijita three rites.
"It may be, sire, that some remorse might arise in you, who desire to perform a great sacrifice, [thinking]:"
‘“A great mass of wealth will surely vanish from me,”’—your Majesty the king should not feel remorse for this.
Furthermore, while your Majesty the king is performing a great sacrifice, there might arise some remorse:
‘“A great mass of wealth will surely vanish from me,”’; your Majesty the king should not feel remorse for this.
"Furthermore, Your Majesty, should some remorse arise in you after having performed the great sacrifice, thinking:
'Alas, my vast mass of wealth has vanished,' that remorse should not be entertained by you, Sire.
These, brahmin, were the three modes that the brahmin family priest taught King Mahāvijita before the sacrifice.
4.5. Ten Aspects.
Then, brahmin, before the sacrifice, the brahmin chaplain dispelled King Mahāvijita’s remorse regarding the recipients in ten ways:
“Sire, there will come to your sacrifice those who take life and those who abstain from taking life.”
Those there who take life, for them it is only by that [act].

But regarding those there who abstain from taking life, may your lordship sacrifice for them, may your lordship prepare for them, may your lordship rejoice for them; may your lordship, within yourself, clarify the mind alone.
There will come to your sacrifice those who take what is not given and those who abstain from taking what is not given... [and so on].
Whether they are those who engage in sexual misconduct or those who abstain from sexual misconduct;
whether they are speakers of falsehood or those who abstain from falsehood;
whether they are speakers of divisive speech or those who abstain from divisive speech...
Whether they are speakers of harsh words or refrain from harsh speech...
whether they are idle talkers or refrain from idle talk...
whether they are covetous or free from covetousness...
Whether their minds are malevolent or non-malevolent...
whether they hold wrong view or right view...
for those among them who hold wrong view, it is only because of that [wrong view].
‘Those among them who possess right view—on their account, may your lordship sacrifice; may your lordship prepare; may your lordship rejoice; may your lordship gladden your own heart within.
In these ten ways, brahmin, did the brahmin family priest dispel King Mahāvijita’s remorse regarding the recipients even before the sacrifice.
4.6. The Sixteen Modes of Dispelment of Remorse.
Then, brahmin, while King Mahāvijita was performing the great sacrifice, the brahmin chaplain instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened his mind with sixteen points, saying:
"It may be that some speaker might say of you, lord King, as you perform this great sacrifice:
'King Mahāvijita performs a great sacrifice, yet he has not invited the khattiyas who are his followers, nor the people of the towns and the countryside.'"
"Yet your majesty the king performs such a great sacrifice.
Even so, there is no one who speaks thus to your majesty the king in accordance with the Dhamma.
For your majesty the king has summoned the khattiyas, the vassals, and the people of both the towns and the countryside.
By this, let your majesty the king know: let your majesty sacrifice, let your majesty prepare, let your majesty rejoice; let your majesty simply settle your own mind within in confidence.
For while your majesty the king is performing this great sacrifice, there might be someone who says:
"King Mahāvijita is indeed sacrificing this great sacrifice, yet his ministers and assembly members have not been invited."
“Both the town-dwellers and the country-folk... both the wealthy brahmins of the towns and the country...
and even the householders and merchants of the towns and the country—yet Your Majesty the King performs such a great sacrifice.
Even in this way, there is no one who speaks to the Lord King in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, the householders, both those from the towns and those from the countryside, have been summoned by the venerable king.
Let the venerable king know this: let him sacrifice, let him prepare, let him rejoice; let the venerable king himself inwardly compose his mind.
However, while the venerable king is performing this great sacrifice, there might be someone who would speak thus:
‘King Mahāvijita is indeed performing a great sacrifice, yet he is not well-born on both sides, from mother and father,
of pure descent for seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth;
and yet this venerable king performs such a great sacrifice.’
"Even so, there is no one who can speak against the lord king in accordance with the Dhamma.
For the lord king is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable by birth.
Let the lord king know this: let the lord sacrifice, let the lord prepare the offerings, let the lord rejoice; let the lord simply find confidence within his own heart."
While the lord king is performing this great sacrifice, there might be someone who says:

"King Mahāvijita is indeed performing a great sacrifice, yet he is not handsome, beautiful, or pleasing; he is not endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, nor does he possess the form of a Brahmā, nor the grace of a Brahmā, nor is he of such noble appearance as to be worth beholding...

[and so on] ...nor is he wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, abundant gold and silver, abundant means of livelihood, abundant wealth and grain, and full treasuries and storehouses... [and so on]."
Nor indeed does he possess a powerful fourfold army that is obedient and responsive to his commands, such that he might prevail over his enemies by means of his glory...

nor indeed is he a faithful giver, a master of generosity, with doors unbarred, acting as a wellspring for ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the beggars, and those who ask, performing meritorious deeds...
nor indeed is he one of great learning regarding various things he has heard...
"Furthermore, he does not understand the meaning of this or that statement, thinking:
'This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement'...
nor is he wise, learned, intelligent, or capable of reflecting upon matters past, future, and present, yet Your Majesty the King performs such a great sacrifice."
In this way, Your Majesty, there is no one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
Moreover, Your Majesty is wise, discerning, intelligent, and capable of considering matters pertaining to the past, the future, and the present.
Let Your Majesty know this by this very fact: let Your Majesty sacrifice, let Your Majesty prepare, let Your Majesty rejoice; let Your Majesty simply settle your own mind within.
While the lord king is performing a great sacrifice, there might be someone who says:
"King Mahāvijita is indeed performing a great sacrifice,
yet his brahmin chaplain is not well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent for seven generations back, unblemished and irreproachable by birth."
"And yet, your majesty the king performs such a great sacrifice.
Even so, there is no one who can speak to your majesty the king in accordance with the Dhamma.

Now, your majesty’s domestic priest, the brahmin, is well-born on both sides, of pure descent from both mother and father, back through seven generations of ancestors, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth.
By this, let your majesty the king know: let your majesty sacrifice, let your majesty prepare, let your majesty rejoice; let your majesty simply settle your own mind within in confidence.
For while your majesty the king is performing this great sacrifice, there might be someone who says:
"King Mahāvijita is indeed sacrificing a great sacrifice."

And yet his chaplain, the brahmin, was not one who had mastered the recitation, was a bearer of the mantras, one who had gone to the further shore of the three Vedas—including the glossaries (nighaṇḍu), the liturgical formulas (keṭubha), the analysis of syllables (sākkharappabheda), and the histories as the fifth—nor was he a master of exegesis, nor was he unskilled in cosmology and the marks of a Great Man... [and so on] ...
nor was his chaplain, the brahmin, virtuous, of mature virtue, or endowed with the virtue of the elders... [and so on].

‘Yet his brahmin chaplain is neither wise, learned, nor intelligent, nor is he the first or second among those who hold up the sacrificial ladle; and yet your majesty the king performs such a great sacrifice.
Even thus, there is no one to speak to your majesty the king in accordance with the Dhamma.
For your majesty’s brahmin chaplain is indeed wise, learned, and intelligent, being the first or second among those who hold up the sacrificial ladle.
"By this, let your majesty the king know: let your majesty sacrifice, let your majesty prepare, let your majesty rejoice; let your majesty simply gladden your own heart within.
In these sixteen ways, brahmin, did the brahmin family priest instruct, exhort, inspire, and encourage the mind of King Mahāvijita as he was performing the great sacrifice.
At that sacrifice, brahmin, neither cattle were slaughtered, nor goats and sheep were slaughtered, nor chickens and pigs...
No living beings were slain, nor did various creatures meet with destruction; no trees were cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts, nor was grass mown for the sake of sacrificial straw.
Even those who were his slaves, messengers, or laborers performed their services not driven by the threat of punishment, nor driven by fear, but rather with tearful faces as they wept.
Then those who wished did so, while those who did not wish did not;
they did what they wished and did not do what they did not wish.
That sacrifice was brought to completion with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses.
Then, brahmin, the kshatriyas— both those from the cities and the countryside— as well as the ministers and councilors—
both those from the cities and the countryside— the wealthy brahmins— both those from the cities and the countryside— and the affluent householders—
both those from the cities and the countryside— took a great deal of wealth, approached King Mahāvijita, and spoke to him thus:
‘Your Majesty, this abundant wealth has been brought specifically for Your Majesty; may Your Majesty accept it.
‘Enough, sir! I too have this abundant wealth, acquired through righteous taxes.
Let that be yours, and bring even more than this!’
Refused by the king, they stepped aside to one side and reflected thus:
“It would not be fitting for us to take these possessions back to our own homes.
King Mahāvijita is performing a great sacrifice; let us become his sacrificial assistants.”
Then, brahmin, to the east of the sacrificial enclosure, the kshatriyas, their followers, and the people of both the towns and the countryside established offerings.
To the south of the sacrificial enclosure, the ministers, the councilors, and the people of both the towns and the countryside established offerings.
To the west of the sacrificial enclosure, the wealthy brahmins and the people of both the towns and the countryside established offerings.
To the north of the sacrificial enclosure, the householders, townspeople, and countryfolk established offerings.
In those sacrifices as well, O brahmin, neither cattle were slain, nor goats and sheep were slain, nor fowl and pigs were slain;
no various living beings were subjected to slaughter, and no trees were cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts.
They gathered reeds for the purpose of sacrificial grass.
Even those who were their slaves, messengers, or laborers performed their services not driven by punishment, nor driven by fear, nor with tearful faces and weeping;
rather, those who wished did so, while those who did not wish did not.
They did what they wished and did not do what they did not wish.
Those sacrifices of theirs reached completion with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curd, honey, and molasses.
Thus there were four who were in favor, and King Mahāvijita was endowed with eight qualities, while the brahmin family priest was endowed with four qualities.
"And the three modes.
This, brahmin, is called the sixteenfold equipment for the perfection of sacrifice.
When this was said, those brahmins became noisy, making a loud clamor and a great din:
“Oh, what a sacrifice! Oh, what a perfection of the sacrifice!
But the brahmin Kūṭadanta remained sitting there in silence.
Then those brahmins said this to the brahmin Kūṭadanta:
“But why, sir, does Master Kūṭadanta not applaud what has been well spoken by the ascetic Gotama as being well spoken?
“I do not fail to applaud what has been well spoken by the ascetic Gotama as being well spoken, sir.
Even one’s head would split apart for anyone who did not applaud what has been well spoken by the ascetic Gotama as being well spoken.”
Moreover, sir, this thought occurs to me:
"The ascetic Gotama does not say,
'Thus have I heard,' nor does he say, 'It ought to be thus.'"
Moreover, the ascetic Gotama speaks thus:
"It was like this at that time; it was just so at that time.
And, sir, this occurs to me:
“Surely, at that time, the ascetic Gotama was either King Mahāvijita or the brahmin priest who officiated at that sacrifice.
“But does Master Gotama recall, having performed or caused such a sacrifice to be performed, being reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a happy destination, in a heavenly world?
“I do recall, brahmin, having performed or caused such a sacrifice to be performed, being reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
“Having passed away from there, I was reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. At that time, I was the brahmin family priest who performed the sacrifice for him.
5. The Sacrifice of Constant Giving and Family Offerings.

“But, Master Gotama, is there another sacrifice that is less troublesome and requires less exertion, yet is more fruitful and more beneficial than this threefold sacrifice with its sixteen requisites?
“There is indeed, brahmin, another sacrifice that is less troublesome and requires less exertion, yet is more fruitful and more beneficial than this threefold sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is that sacrifice which is less troublesome and less laborious, yet more fruitful and more beneficial than this threefold sacrifice with its sixteen requisites?
“Now, brahmin, those perpetual gifts and family sacrifices which are given to virtuous renunciants;”

“This, brahmin, is the sacrifice that— compared to this threefold perfection of sacrifice with sixteen requisites— is less costly, requires less effort, yet yields greater fruit and brings greater benefit. “But what, Master Gotama,
is the cause and what is the reason why that perpetual giving, that sacrifice for one’s own kin,
is less costly and requires less effort than this threefold perfection of sacrifice with sixteen requisites?”
“...which is more fruitful and brings greater benefit?
“Brahmin, neither Arahants nor those who have entered the path to Arahantship approach such a sacrifice. Why is that?”
"Here, brahmin, one sees blows with sticks and even throttling by the throat; therefore, Arahants or those who have entered the path to arahantship do not approach such a sacrifice.

But as for those regular gifts, brahmin, those family sacrifices given in honor of virtuous renunciants—it is to such a sacrifice, brahmin, that Arahants or those who have entered the path to arahantship do approach."
For what reason?
Because here, brahmin, no blows with sticks or throat-seizures are seen; therefore, arahants or those who have entered the path to arahantship approach such a sacrifice.
This, brahmin, is the cause, this is the condition, by which that perpetual gift, that family sacrifice, [is sustained] through these three kinds...
“Which sacrifice is more excellent and less troublesome, more fruitful and more beneficial than this perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites? “But,
Master Gotama, is there another sacrifice that is superior to this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites?”
“Is this constant giving, this sacrifice performed for one’s own kin, less fruitful and less meritorious than that which is more excellent and requires less exertion?
“There is indeed, brahmin, another sacrifice that surpasses this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.”
“Moreover, this constant giving, this sacrifice performed for one’s own kin, is less troublesome, requires less effort,
yet yields greater fruit and greater benefit.
“But what, Master Gotama, is that sacrifice which is superior to these three kinds of sacrificial success and the sixteen requisites of sacrifice?”
“Is this constant giving, this sacrifice performed for one’s own kin, less fruitful and less beneficial, yet more productive of great fruit and greater advantage than that?
“Brahmin, he who builds a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters— this, brahmin, [is indeed more fruitful].”
“A sacrifice [performed] with this threefold perfection of sacrifice, these sixteen requisites, and this constant giving as a family sacrifice,
is more excellent, involves less trouble, and yields greater fruit and greater benefit. “But, Master Gotama,
is there another sacrifice that is even more excellent than this threefold perfection of sacrifice, these sixteen requisites, and this constant giving as a family sacrifice?”
“Is this constant giving, this ancestral sacrifice, and this gift of a monastery more fruitful and more beneficial—
requiring less effort and involving less exertion—
than that? “There is indeed, brahmin, another sacrifice that surpasses these three kinds of sacrificial success and the sixteen requisites.”
“Compared to this constant giving, this ancestral sacrifice, and this gift of a monastery, [the latter] is more excellent, requires less effort,
and yields greater fruit and greater benefit.
“But what, Master Gotama, is that sacrifice which is superior to these three kinds of sacrificial perfection and the sixteen requisites?”
“Is this constant giving, this ancestral sacrifice, and this gift of a monastery less fruitful and less meritorious than that?
“Brahmin, whoever with a confident heart goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha;”
“Indeed, brahmin, this sacrifice is less troublesome and less laborious,
yet more fruitful and more beneficial than this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites,
than this perpetual giving and family sacrifice, and than this gift of a monastery.”
“But, Master Gotama, is there another sacrifice that is less costly and requires less effort,

yet yields greater fruit and greater benefit than this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites, this perpetual giving as a family sacrifice, this gift of a monastery, and these goings for refuge?”
“There is, brahmin, another sacrifice that is less costly and requires less effort,

yet yields greater fruit and brings greater benefit than this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites, than this constant giving and family sacrifice, and than this gift of a monastery and these goings for refuge.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is that sacrifice which is less costly and requires less effort,

yet is more fruitful and more beneficial than this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites, than this perpetual giving and family sacrifice, and than this gift of a monastery and these goings for refuge?”
“Brahmin, when one with a confident heart undertakes the training rules—

abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
this, brahmin, is the sacrifice that surpasses this threefold sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.”
“Compared to constant giving, to the ancestral sacrifice, and to this gift of a monastery, as well as these acts of going for refuge,
this [gift] is less costly, requires less effort, yet yields greater fruit and brings greater benefit. “But, Master Gotama,
is there another sacrifice that is superior to this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites?”
“Is this constant giving, this ancestral sacrifice, this gift of a monastery, these goings for refuge,
and these training precepts— compared to these— less troublesome, less arduous, yet more fruitful and more beneficial? “There is indeed, brahmin,
another sacrifice that surpasses this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites.”
“By this constant giving, by this ancestral sacrifice, by this gift of a monastery, by these goings for refuge,

and by these training rules— [the latter] is less costly, requires less effort, yet is more fruitful and more beneficial. “But what, Master Gotama, is that sacrifice which, compared to this threefold perfection of sacrifice with its sixteen requisites, [is superior]?”
“Is this constant giving, this ancestral sacrifice, and this gift of a monastery,
along with these goings for refuge and these training rules, less costly and less troublesome, yet more fruitful and more beneficial? “In this case, brahmin,
a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One … [as in the standard formula] …”
"In this way, brahmin, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This sacrifice, brahmin, is more excellent and less troublesome than the previous sacrifices, and it is of greater fruit and greater benefit... [as before]..."
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna.
“This too, brahmin, is a sacrifice that is less costly and less troublesome than the previous sacrifices, yet more fruitful and more beneficial.
… [omission] … He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision.
“This too, brahmin, is a sacrifice that is less costly and less troublesome than the previous sacrifices, yet more fruitful and more beneficial. … [omission] …
"He understands: 'There is no further state of being.
This sacrifice, brahmin, is indeed more excellent and less troublesome than previous sacrifices; it is of greater fruit and greater benefit.
And, brahmin, there is no other perfection of sacrifice that is superior or more sublime than this perfection of sacrifice."
6. The Declaration of Kūṭadanta’s Admission as a Lay Follower When this was said, the brahmin Kūṭadanta addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!”
"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways."
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And I, sir Gotama, [give] seven hundred bulls, seven hundred young bulls, and seven hundred heifers.
"I release seven hundred goats and seven hundred rams; I grant them their lives.
Let them eat green grass, let them drink cool water, and let a cool breeze blow upon them.
7. The Realization of the Fruit of Stream-Entry.
Then the Blessed One gave a gradual discourse to the brahmin Kūṭadanta, namely:
a talk on generosity, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that the brahmin Kūṭadanta had a ready mind, a pliable mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, then he revealed that teaching of the Dhamma which is uniquely proclaimed by Buddhas.
Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take up the dye, even so, while still on that very seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose for the brahmin Kūṭadanta: [that all things subject to origination are subject to cessation].
“Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.
Then the brahmin Kūṭadanta, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;
having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained intrepidity, and no longer dependent on others in the Teacher’s dispensation, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“May the Blessed Gotama accept my meal tomorrow, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the brahmin Kūṭadanta, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, at the end of that night, the brahmin Kūṭadanta had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own sacrificial enclosure. When it was time, he had the Blessed One informed:
"It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to the brahmin Kūṭadanta’s sacrificial enclosure. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him.
Then the brahmin Kūṭadanta, with his own hands, served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard foods and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin Kūṭadanta took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As the brahmin Kūṭadanta was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
The Kūṭadantasutta, the fifth, is finished.
